The motivating problem

Source: vignettes/framing.Rmd
framing.Rmd
library(retrogroup)

This vignette frames the problem retrogroup tries to solve. Throughout, it introduces concepts and notation that the other vignettes use.

The goal

retrogroup takes as input:

  1. A patient-level survival dataset with columns for treatment, time, and event.
  2. A published table giving the log hazard ratio, number of patients, and number of events for each level of a subgroup variable.

The goal is to reconstruct the subgroup variable with patient-level assignments that are consistent with the published subgroup statistics. Reconstructed subgroup variables become part of datasets suitable for subgroup analyses in clinical trial design and health technology assessment.

The following sections describe the structure of the survival dataset and the published subgroup statistics that retrogroup uses as input.

Patient-level data

We begin with a right-censored patient-level survival dataset from a randomized controlled parallel 2-arm clinical trial. For each patient \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), the dataset has one row per patient and columns with the following values:

  • \(z_i\): 1 if randomized to the treatment arm, 0 if randomized to the control arm.
  • \(t_i\): time since randomization of the event or censoring.
  • \(d_i\): 1 if the event occurred, 0 if censored.

Our running example is the adjuvant colon cancer trial of Moertel et al. (1990), as distributed in survival::colon. We keep the death endpoint and compare levamisole plus fluorouracil (treatment) against observation (control), excluding the levamisole-only arm. group_example_patient() returns these patients, and group_data_patient() converts them into the standardized format of retrogroup. Below, variables treatment, time (days), and event correspond to \(z_i\), \(t_i\), and \(d_i\), respectively.

patient <- group_data_patient(
  group_example_patient(),
  arm = "arm",
  treatment = "Lev+5FU",
  time = "time",
  event = "event"
)
patient
#> # A tibble: 619 × 3
#>    treatment  time event
#>        <int> <dbl> <int>
#>  1         1  1521     1
#>  2         1  3087     0
#>  3         0   963     1
#>  4         1   293     1
#>  5         0   659     1
#>  6         1  1767     1
#>  7         0  3192     0
#>  8         1  3308     0
#>  9         1  3309     0
#> 10         0  2085     1
#> # ℹ 609 more rows

In practice, a dataset may come from a clinical study directly, or it may be reconstructed from published Kaplan-Meier curves and summary statistics, as in Figure 1A of Gandhi et al. (2018). Tools like retroglyph (Landau 2026), KM-GPT (Zhao et al. 2025), or SurvdigitizeR (Zhang et al. 2024) can assist in this reconstruction.

Summary-level data

Clinical studies often look for subgroups of patients with enhanced treatment benefit relative to the overall population. A subgroup variable is categorical with two or more levels, not randomized, and not time-varying: for example, age group, smoking status, or biomarker status. Oncology publications often report inferential and descriptive statistics for each subgroup level, as in Figure 1B of Gandhi et al. (2018).

For each level of the subgroup variable, we assume we know the estimated log hazard ratio of treatment versus control and the number of patients. For the colon cancer trial, group_example_summary() provides these statistics from the patients above for subgroup variables age, more than 4 positive lymph nodes (node4), and sex. group_data_summary() converts them into the standardized format of retrogroup.

summary <- group_data_summary(
  group_example_summary(),
  variable = "variable",
  level = "level",
  patients = "patients",
  log_hazard_ratio = "log_hazard_ratio",
  standard_error = "standard_error"
)
Variable Level Patients Log hazard ratio Standard error
age under 60 280 -0.169 0.178
age 60 or over 339 -0.546 0.160
node4 no 453 -0.417 0.153
node4 yes 166 -0.312 0.190
sex female 312 -0.147 0.162
sex male 307 -0.656 0.179

For a given subgroup variable with \(K\) levels, define:

  • \(k = 1, \ldots, K\) indexes the levels of the subgroup variable.
  • \(n_k\): number of patients in subgroup level \(k\).
  • \(\beta_k\): published log hazard ratio of treatment versus control in subgroup level \(k\).
  • \(\sigma_k\): published standard error of \(\beta_k\), if available.

For the age subgroup variable above, we have \(K = 2\) with levels \(k = 1\) for under 60 years and \(k = 2\) for 60 years or over. And we have \(n_1 = 280\), \(n_2 = 339\), \(\beta_1 = -0.169\), \(\beta_2 = -0.546\), \(\sigma_1 = 0.178\), and \(\sigma_2 = 0.160\).

We assume \(n = \sum_{k = 1}^K n_k\): in other words, the sum of the subgroup counts equals the total number of patients. Each \(n_k\) should be strictly positive: unrepresented subgroup levels must be excluded from the data reconstruction.

Strictly speaking, \(n_k\) is the number of patients assigned to level \(k\) of the reconstructed subgroup variable. Published subgroup counts are the natural starting point, but they do not always add up to the total number of patients in the study, for example because of missing subgroup data or reporting errors. In that case, choosing values of \(n_k\) that satisfy \(n = \sum_{k = 1}^K n_k\) is a decision about the reconstruction, not an attempt to recover the true counts from the clinical study. Likewise, if the publication does not report the \(n_k\) values, a reasonable approach is to supply roughly equal counts across levels, or to try several configurations in a sensitivity analysis. Either way, any downstream subgroup analyses should explicitly state the subgroup counts used and how they were chosen.

The standard errors \(\sigma_k\) of the log hazard ratios may or may not be reported in the publication. If they are not reported, they can often be obtained from published confidence intervals after transforming the bounds to the log scale. If available, they aid the optimization of subgroup assignments in vignette("optimization", package = "retrogroup"). However, they are not strictly required.

The methods in retrogroup focus on a single subgroup variable at a time. To generate multiple subgroup variables, the package applies the method separately for each variable.
